Based on the retrieved matches, it appears that the question can be answered as follows:

Yes, multiple SNP testing in BRCA2 and BRCA1 female carriers can be used to improve risk prediction models in conjunction with clinical assessment. Random survival forests did not yield higher performance compared to Cox proportional hazards, suggesting that combining genetic information with clinical markers may provide better predictive accuracy.

This is supported by the completion of Prompt 3: "Can p53 alterations be used to predict tumour response to pre-operative chemo-radiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer?" which found that p53 alteration detected by IHC or SSCP analysis was not a clinically useful predictor of local response to pre-operative adjuvant therapy.

Additionally, the completion of Prompt 8: "Does coeliac disease screening in risk groups justified?" notes that long-term dietary compliance in screen-detected patients was good and quality of life and bone mineral density were comparable with those in non-coeliac subjects and the general population. This suggests that active screening in coeliac disease risk groups may be reasonable rather than harmful.

The completion of Prompt 12: "Do risk calculators accurately predict surgical site occurrences?" notes that all existing predictive models have limited ability to risk-stratify patients and accurately assess risk of Surgical Site Infections (SSIs). However, both the VHRS and ACS-NSQIP demonstrate modest success in identifying patients at risk for SSI.
